facts.statement: Triceratops was a very large animal, measuring approximately 8 to 9 meters in length and weighing up to 6 to 10 metric tons.
facts.quote: Triceratops was a very large animal, measuring around 8 - 9 m in length and weighing up to 6 - 10 MT.

facts.statement: A specific T. horridus specimen named Kelsey measured 22 to 24 feet long, had a 6.5-foot skull, stood 7.5 feet tall, and was estimated to weigh 5.4 metric tons.
facts.quote: A specimen of T. horridus named Kelsey measured 22 - 24 ft long, has a 6.5 ft skull, stood about 7.5 ft tall, and was estimated by the Black Hills Institute to weigh approximately 5.4 MT.

facts.statement: A T. horridus specimen named Big John was estimated to be 26.1 feet long and 10 feet tall.
facts.quote: A T. horridus specimen named Big John was estimated to have been 26.1 ft long and 10 ft tall.

facts.statement: The largest known Triceratops skull, specimen MWC 7584, was estimated to be 2.5 meters long when complete, reaching nearly one-third of the animal's total length.
facts.quote: The largest-known skull, specimen MWC 7584 (formerly BYU 12183), is estimated to have been 2.5 m in length when complete and could reach almost a third of the length of the entire animal.

facts.statement: Triceratops had a large beak located at the front of its head, in front of its teeth.
facts.quote: The front of the head was equipped with a large beak in front of its teeth.

facts.statement: Triceratops possessed a single horn on its snout located above the nostrils.
facts.quote: The skull bore a single horn on the snout above the nostrils.

facts.statement: The skull roof of Triceratops was created by fused bones and a folding of the frontal bones, resulting in a double-layered structure.
facts.quote: The bones of the skull roof were fused and by a folding of the frontal bones, a "double" skull roof was created.

facts.statement: Triceratops had a relatively short bony frill at the rear of the skull formed by the squamosal and parietal bones, which featured epoccipitals in young specimens.
facts.quote: At the rear of the skull, the outer squamosal bones and the inner parietal bones grew into a relatively short, bony frill, adorned with epoccipitals in young specimens.

facts.statement: Unlike most other ceratopsids which had large openings in their frills, the frills of Triceratops were noticeably solid, though this may vary if Torosaurus represents mature Triceratops individuals.
facts.quote: Most other ceratopsids had large parietal fenestrae, openings in their frills, but those of Triceratops were noticeably solid, unless the genus Torosaurus represents mature Triceratops individuals, which it most likely does not.

facts.statement: The Triceratops vertebral column consisted of ten neck vertebrae, twelve back vertebrae, ten sacral vertebrae, and about forty-five tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: The vertebral column consisted of ten neck, twelve back, ten sacral, and about forty-five tail vertebrae.

facts.statement: In Triceratops, the spinous processes of the neck remained constant in height and did not gradually slope upwards.
facts.quote: In Triceratops, the spinous processes of the neck are constant in height and don't gradually slope upwards.

facts.statement: While Triceratops was certainly quadrupedal, its posture is debated; originally believed to have sprawling front legs, evidence now suggests an upright stance with elbows flexed behind, similar to a modern rhinoceros.
facts.quote: Although certainly quadrupedal, the posture of horned dinosaurs has long been the subject of some debate. Originally, it was believed that the front legs of the animal had to be sprawling at a considerable angle from the thorax in order to better bear the weight of the head. This stance can be seen in paintings by Charles Knight and Rudolph Zallinger. Ichnological evidence in the form of trackways from horned dinosaurs and recent reconstructions of skeletons (both physical and digital) seem to show that Triceratops and other ceratopsids maintained an upright stance during normal locomotion, with the elbows flexed to behind and slightly bowed out, in an intermediate state between fully upright and fully sprawling, comparable to the modern rhinoceros.

facts.statement: The phalangeal formula of the Triceratops hand is 2-3-4-3-1, indicating the number of bones in each finger of the forelimb.
facts.quote: The phalangeal formula of the hand is 2-3-4-3-1, meaning that the first or innermost finger of the forelimb has two bones, the next has three, the next has four, etc.

facts.statement: The basement scales covering most of the Triceratops body are large, with the largest known in ceratopsians reaching up to 9 cm across.
facts.quote: The basement scales covering the majority of the body are large in size, the largest known in ceratopsians at up to 9 cm across.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest it is unlikely that the nipple-like projections on Triceratops feature scales bore bristles like those found in other ceratopsians.
facts.quote: It has been suggested that it is unlikely that the nipple-like projections of the feature scales bore bristles like those known in other ceratopsians like Psittacosaurus.

facts.statement: Thomas Lehman defined the subfamilies in 1990 and diagnosed Triceratops as a "ceratopsine" based on several morphological features.
facts.quote: Thomas Lehman defining both subfamilies in 1990 and diagnosing Triceratops as "ceratopsine" on the basis of several morphological features.

facts.statement: In 2012, a group of three Triceratops of varying sizes from adult to juvenile were found near Newcastle, Wyoming.

facts.statement: Remains of Triceratops show signs of predation or scavenging by Tyrannosaurus, particularly on the largest specimen, with breakage and puncture wounds on the front limb bones.

facts.statement: Analysis of endocranial anatomy suggests Triceratops had a poor sense of smell compared to other dinosaurs.

facts.statement: An isotopic analysis study suggests Triceratops was gigantothermic, or possibly endothermic due to its large body volume.
